Baby & Child

Dry eyes in children: symptoms, eye tests and care

Updated: November 4, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A child who keeps blinking, rubbing their eyes or saying that they feel sandy may have an irritated eye surface. Dry eye is one possibility, but allergy, infection, an injury or a focusing problem can look similar. An assessment can identify what is happening and choose care that fits the child's age, comfort and daily life.

Recognize symptoms without assuming the cause

Dry eye means the tear film does not keep the eye surface adequately protected. There may be too little tear production, excessive evaporation or problems with how tears spread. Burning, grittiness, redness, watering and vision that comes and goes can occur; an eye that waters is not necessarily well lubricated.

Younger children may rub, blink repeatedly, squint or avoid tasks rather than describe dryness. Note when this happens, whether one or both eyes are affected and any crusting or trouble seeing. Persistent symptoms deserve an eye appointment. Do not use the absence of a detailed complaint to decide that a child is comfortable, or label all rubbing as dry eye.

Get urgent help for warning signs

A very painful red eye or a red eye in a contact-lens wearer needs urgent assessment. A newborn under 28 days with red eyes also needs urgent medical help. A child under two with a red eye should be assessed rather than treated by trial and error. Seek advice sooner if the child is unwell or you are concerned.

A red eye with a new change in sight, pain when looking at light, an injury or chemical exposure needs emergency eye care. Severe headache with nausea, a newly unequal pupil or an extremely dark-red eye also needs emergency assessment. These signs should not wait for lubricants or a screen break to work. Arrange appropriate transport; do not drive yourself if your own vision or condition makes it unsafe.

Prepare for a child-friendly eye examination

Tell the eye-care professional about symptom timing, lenses, screens, allergies, skin or joint problems, other illnesses and all medicines or drops. Bring product names and describe effects on reading, school, sleep or play. The clinician may check sight, eyelids, blinking, the cornea and tear film, looking for causes beyond dryness.

Tests are selected for the child's age and ability to cooperate. A slit lamp is a microscope with a narrow bright light for examining the eye and eyelids. A dye may help show the tear film or surface damage; pupil-dilating drops are used when the wider examination calls for them, not because every dry-eye assessment requires the same drops. Ask how to help the child feel comfortable.

Understand tear tests and their limits

A Schirmer test uses a small paper strip near the lower eyelid to measure how much it becomes wet over several minutes. It can help assess tear production, but discomfort and reflex tearing may affect results. Some children cannot comfortably complete it, and other tests may be more appropriate. It is not a home test or a single answer to every child's symptoms.

Tear break-up time, or TBUT, measures how long the tear film remains stable after a blink, sometimes with dye and sometimes using noninvasive equipment. Surface staining can show irritated or damaged areas. Adult cutoffs and questionnaires do not automatically work in children; recent pediatric research still identifies important measurement limits. The clinician interprets the findings together rather than diagnosing from a universal ten-second rule.

Review ordinary contact lenses when they are uncomfortable

Lenses can contribute to discomfort, but a poorly fitting lens, allergy, surface damage or infection may be responsible. Remove uncomfortable lenses, use glasses and contact the eye-care professional; do not put them back until advised. Redness, worsening pain, light sensitivity, sudden blur or unusual discharge calls for immediate advice, not simply buying a wetter lens.

After checking the eye, the clinician may adjust fit, material, wearing time, cleaning or replacement schedule, or recommend a pause. Daily disposables or another material can suit some children, but no type guarantees relief. Follow the prescribed cleaning and wear instructions and use only drops compatible with the particular lenses. Specialist therapeutic lenses are a separate treatment choice.

Make screen use easier on the eyes

Children often blink less while concentrating on a phone, game or school screen. This can allow tears to evaporate and contribute to discomfort, but a screen history does not establish the diagnosis. Encourage full blinking, comfortable lighting and a screen at a sensible distance, with breaks built into schoolwork and leisure.

The 20–20–20 reminder means looking about 20 feet, or six metres, away for 20 seconds every 20 minutes. It is a practical break habit rather than a cure or a test. Balance screen time with other activities and avoid direct fan or air-conditioning flow at the eyes. Persistent pain, headaches, blurred or double vision still needs an eye examination.

Treat eyelid inflammation with an individual plan

Blepharitis is inflammation around the eyelid margins. Meibomian glands there supply oils that help tears function; when they are inflamed or blocked, crusting, burning, watering or fluctuating blur can accompany dryness. This is more than simply having bacteria on the lashes, and allergy or skin conditions may contribute.

The clinician may demonstrate a comfortably warm, never hot, compress and gentle cleaning along the closed lid margins. Ask about the product, pressure and frequency for your child; do not scrub the eyeball or press hard on the lids. Some children need prescribed treatment and follow-up. Office cleaning or heating procedures, including branded treatments, are not automatically appropriate or proven safe for every age.

Consider health conditions and medicines when relevant

Persistent or severe dryness sometimes accompanies an autoimmune condition such as Sjögren's disease or juvenile idiopathic arthritis, diabetes, or a congenital problem affecting tears, eyelids or corneal sensation. Nutritional deficiency can also affect the eye surface. These are reasons for a careful history and selected assessment, not a reason to assume that every child needs extensive blood tests.

Allergy medicines, acne retinoids, some medicines for depression and certain preserved eye drops may contribute. Tell the prescriber about new eye symptoms and when they began. A supervised change may help, but do not stop a prescribed treatment yourself. The pediatric and eye-care teams can coordinate treatment of an underlying condition while protecting the eye surface.

Choose lubricants for the child and the diagnosis

Artificial tears can improve comfort, and some children need a gel or ointment. Ask an eye-care professional or pharmacist which product and schedule are appropriate, particularly for an infant or a child with other eye disease. Preservative-free preparations may be preferable with frequent use or sensitivity, but the label alone does not make every bottle suitable for every child.

Wash hands, keep the dropper tip from touching the eye or skin and follow storage and after-opening expiry instructions. Ask for a demonstration if giving drops is difficult, and how to space different prescribed products. Do not share drops, use homemade mixtures or substitute redness-whitening drops for lubricants. Increasing drops should not conceal persistent pain or a change in sight.

Keep food and supplement claims in perspective

A varied, age-appropriate diet supports health. A very restricted diet, poor growth, malabsorption or suspected vitamin deficiency deserves pediatric advice, because a genuine deficiency needs proper assessment and treatment. This is different from promising that extra vitamins C or E will prevent tears from evaporating.

Omega-3 supplements are sometimes discussed for eyelid or dry-eye problems, but they are not a guaranteed treatment. A large adult dry-eye trial found no benefit over placebo; it does not establish a dose or benefit for children. Discuss any supplement with the child's clinician, including allergies and other medicines, rather than using high-dose vitamins or fish oil in place of eye care.

Prescription and office treatments need specialist oversight

If lubrication and treatment of the cause are insufficient, an ophthalmologist may consider anti-inflammatory drops or other targeted treatment. The choice depends on the diagnosis, age, local approval and monitoring needs. Antibiotics may be used for selected eyelid problems; they are not a routine cure for every dry eye.

Steroid eye drops can raise eye pressure and cause other harm, so they must not be borrowed or started without supervision. An office eyelid procedure should be discussed in terms of the child's ability to cooperate, evidence, discomfort, alternatives and follow-up. Pediatric evidence is less complete than adult evidence, and no branded device should be presented as an inevitable next step.

Punctal plugs can retain tears in selected cases

Tiny plugs can partly block the drainage openings at the inner eyelid corners, keeping tears on the eye longer. This is different from opening a newborn's blocked tear duct. An eye specialist may consider plugs for persistent, significant dryness after assessing the surface and the response to other care.

Small pediatric case series report benefit, but do not guarantee results or safety for every child. Plugs may fall out, symptoms may return and repeat treatment can be needed. Placement may require anaesthesia depending on age and cooperation. Ask why plugs suit this child, what problems to report and how their position and eye health will be checked.

Specialist scleral lenses are not permanent implants

Severe ocular-surface disease may sometimes be managed with a custom scleral device, including PROSE. A gas-permeable dome rests on the white of the eye and arches over the cornea, holding a fluid reservoir against the surface. It is fitted by a specialist and is different from routinely changing ordinary contact-lens brands.

These devices are removable; they are not permanent lenses implanted in the eye. Care involves trained application, removal, cleaning and the prescribed sterile filling solution, usually with removal at bedtime. Selected children with severe disease have benefited, but fitting or daily handling is not feasible for everyone. Evidence from serious conditions such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome cannot promise the same result for ordinary childhood dryness.

Plan follow-up around comfort, sight and daily life

Agree on how long to try the chosen care, when to return and which changes require earlier help. A simple note about symptoms, drops and school difficulties may be useful. If a routine is painful, takes too much time or is difficult for the child to tolerate, tell the team so it can be adapted rather than silently abandoned.

The aim is a comfortable, protected eye surface and clear vision while identifying and managing the cause. Do not keep treating presumed dryness indefinitely when symptoms persist. New pain, light sensitivity or visual change deserves prompt reassessment, and the emergency signs described above should bypass the routine follow-up plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Arrange an eye assessment for persistent symptoms and describe the child's vision, comfort, medicines and daily activities.

Use an individual plan for the identified cause, with demonstrated care and clear instructions for drops or other treatments.

Keep follow-up and act promptly on pain, light sensitivity or visual change rather than waiting for routine care to work.

How BeMama can help

BeMama helps you prepare questions and organize the child's care plan; symptoms and treatment choices still need an appropriate eye examination.

When to seek help

Do not diagnose a child's red or painful eye from an online guide. Newborn red eyes, painful red eyes and contact-lens redness need urgent assessment. Red eyes with sight changes, light pain, injury or chemical exposure need emergency care. Do not use borrowed steroid drops or stop prescribed medicines yourself.

Evidence notes updated: November 4, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Rubbing, blinking or watering can have several causes; persistent symptoms need assessment.
  • Tear tests must be interpreted for the child, not through one adult cutoff.
  • Screens, lenses, eyelid inflammation, medicines and other conditions may contribute.
  • Use child-appropriate care and specialist oversight for prescriptions, plugs or therapeutic lenses.
  • Pain, light sensitivity or a new change in sight must not be dismissed as dryness.

Frequently asked questions

How is dry eye diagnosed in a child?

The clinician combines symptoms, sight and eye-surface examination with selected tear tests. Schirmer testing measures paper wetting, while TBUT assesses tear stability. Age and cooperation affect interpretation; no single test proves every case.

Can contact lenses cause a teenager's dry eyes?

They can contribute, but infection, allergy or a fit problem may look similar. Remove uncomfortable lenses and obtain advice. Redness, pain, light sensitivity, sudden blur or discharge needs immediate eye-care contact; do not simply switch brands.

What signs might a baby or child show?

Frequent blinking, rubbing, squinting, grittiness, redness, watering or fluctuating blur may occur. They are not specific to dryness. A newborn with red eyes needs urgent assessment, and pain or apparent difficulty seeing needs prompt help.

Can prolonged phone or computer use make eyes dry?

Reduced blinking during concentrated screen use can contribute. Regular distance breaks, full blinking and a comfortable setup may help, but persistent symptoms still need examination rather than being blamed automatically on screens.

Can I choose any preservative-free eye drop?

No. Ask about a suitable lubricant for the child's age and condition and follow its instructions. Preservative-free products can help with frequent use or sensitivity, but do not replace assessment or make every formulation appropriate.

Should I give omega-3 or extra vitamins?

Do not assume supplements will treat dryness. Discuss a restricted diet or suspected deficiency with the clinician. Benefits of supplements for pediatric dry eye are uncertain, and products can have risks or interactions.

Are punctal plugs and PROSE routine treatments?

No. They are options for selected cases under specialist care. Plugs retain tears but can be lost or need replacement; custom scleral devices need fitting and daily handling. Neither guarantees a result for every child.

When should we seek emergency eye care?

A red eye with new sight changes, pain looking at light, injury or chemical exposure needs emergency assessment. Severe headache with nausea or a newly unequal pupil also needs urgent emergency attention. A very painful red eye, a red contact-lens eye or red eyes in a newborn needs urgent medical assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
